title: Malik's Mural: Multiplying Big Numbers
goal: I can estimate first, then multiply 2-digit and 3-digit numbers by 2-digit numbers step by step and check my answer.

card.desc: You connect the area model you already know to stacked partial products and the standard algorithm (18 × 13 = 180 + 54 = 234). You estimate first, line up the 0 in the tens row, regroup carefully, add the rows, and find the mistake in someone else's work, all with Malik's tile mural from Pathways Week 6.

win: You estimated, stacked, regrouped and checked. Malik's mural is ready to order!

slides.title: Malik's Mural: Multiplying Big Numbers
slides.text: Malik's art class is painting a giant tile mural on the gym wall. The mural is 24 tiles across and 18 tiles down. Today you learn to find that number fast and get it right every time.

notes.do: Before class: grid paper (1 cm squares), 2 colored pencils, scissors, whiteboard and marker, pencil and scrap paper. Ethan writes every problem on paper today, even the ones he types.
notes.say: Today is all about one big skill: multiplying 2-digit and 3-digit numbers, step by step, so you get it right the first time. Slow is fast today.
notes.ask: What do you remember about the area model from Multiplication Mountain?
notes.listen: Split a number into tens and ones, multiply each part, add the parts. He knows this idea well; today we connect it to the stacked method.

slides.title: Malik's problem
slides.text: The mural is 24 tiles across and 18 tiles down. Malik has to order the exact number of tiles.
prompts: Why is counting the tiles one by one a bad plan?
Why should Malik get the exact number and not just a guess?
What do you think the answer is close to? How did you decide?
starters: Counting one by one is slow because …
I think it is close to … because …

notes.do: Let him talk for 2 to 3 minutes. Write his guess for 24 × 18 in the corner of the whiteboard. We come back to it later.
notes.ask: If Malik orders too few tiles, what happens? Too many?
notes.listen: Too few means the mural is unfinished; too many wastes money. If he says about 400 (20 × 20), praise it: that is an estimate, and we will use it.

slides.title: Facts and tens
slides.text: Type each answer. These are the building blocks for today.

items.no: 40 is 4 tens. Do 4 × 6, then keep the zero.
Times 10 makes each digit worth ten times more.
Do 3 × 2, then count the zeros in both factors.
items.hint: 3 × 2 = 6. There are two zeros in 30 and 20.

notes.do: He answers out loud first, then types. Fast and confident is the goal.
notes.listen: One zero from 30 and one from 20. 3 tens × 2 tens = 6 hundreds.

slides.title: Words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word, the meaning and the example out loud.

words.meaning: The answer to a multiplication problem.
One piece of a multiplication problem. You find each piece, then add the pieces.
A smart guess you make by rounding first. It tells you about how big the answer should be.
To carry extra value into the next place-value column when a column makes 10 or more.
words.example: 8 × 4 = 32, so I write the 2 and regroup the 3 tens.

words.meaning: The stacked, step-by-step way to multiply bigger numbers on paper.
words.example: The standard algorithm does the same math as the area model, just stacked.

words.meaning: The answer to a division problem.

notes.do: He reads each card aloud, then covers the card and says the meaning in his own words.
notes.say: Today you will not pick these words from a list. You will type them from memory, so say each one out loud.
notes.ask: Which two words are the answers? (product for multiplying, quotient for dividing.) What is the difference between a product and a partial product?
notes.listen: A partial product is one piece; the product is the whole answer after you add the pieces.

slides.title: Estimate first
slides.text: Before you multiply, estimate. Round each factor to the nearest ten, then multiply.

steps.text: 18 × 13. 18 rounds to 20. 13 rounds to 10.
If you get 23 or 2,340, something went wrong. Those are not close to 200.
The estimate is your alarm. If your answer is far away from it, go back and find the mistake.

slides.tip: An estimate is not the answer. It tells you about how big the answer should be.

notes.do: Click the steps one at a time. Write 18 × 13 ≈ 20 × 10 = 200 on the whiteboard.
notes.say: Every problem today starts with an estimate. It takes five seconds and it catches the biggest mistakes.
notes.ask: Why is 2,340 not reasonable? Why is 23 not reasonable?
notes.listen: 2,340 is about ten times too big (an extra zero). 23 is far too small; multiplying 18 by 13 must give more than 18 × 10 = 180.

items.q: Round both factors to the nearest ten. Estimate 47 × 22: 50 × 20 = ____
Malik's notes show four answers for 24 × 18. Estimate: 20 × 20 = 400. Which answer is reasonable?
items.why: 432 is close to the estimate of 400.
no: 42 is just 24 + 18. That is adding, not multiplying.
4,320 is about ten times too big. Look for an extra zero.
192 is only 24 × 8. It leaves out the 24 × 10 piece.

notes.do: He says the estimate out loud before he answers.
notes.ask: For the second one, what mistake made 192? What made 4,320?
notes.listen: 192 = only one partial product (24 × 8). 4,320 = an extra zero. These are the exact mistakes we hunt today.

slides.title: The area model: 18 × 13
slides.text: You already know this one. Split both factors: 18 = 10 + 8 and 13 = 10 + 3.

steps.text: Draw 2 columns (10 and 8) and 2 rows (10 and 3). That makes 4 boxes.

<svg viewBox="0 0 324 220" width="100%" style="max-width:344px;display:block;margin:auto" font-family="Fredoka,sans-serif"><text x="131.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">10</text><text x="266.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">8</text><text x="36" y="92.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">10</text><rect x="46" y="34" width="170" height="104" fill="#F3F8FF" stroke="#0047BA" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="93.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" fill="#0A1F3D">100</text><rect x="216" y="34" width="100" height="104" fill="#F3F8FF" stroke="#0047BA" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="93.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" fill="#0A1F3D">80</text><text x="36" y="181.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">3</text><rect x="46" y="138" width="170" height="74" fill="#F3F8FF" stroke="#0047BA" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="182.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" fill="#0A1F3D">30</text><rect x="216" y="138" width="100" height="74" fill="#F3F8FF" stroke="#0047BA" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="182.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" fill="#0A1F3D">24</text></svg>

steps.text: Add each row: top row 100 + 80 = 180 (that is 18 × 10). Bottom row 30 + 24 = 54 (that is 18 × 3).
Those two rows are the partial products: 18 × 10 = 180 and 18 × 3 = 54.

visual.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 424 220" width="100%" style="max-width:444px;display:block;margin:auto" font-family="Fredoka,sans-serif"><text x="131.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">10</text><text x="266.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">8</text><text x="36" y="92.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">10</text><rect x="46" y="34" width="170" height="104" fill="#F3F8FF" stroke="#0047BA" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="93.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" fill="#0A1F3D">100</text><rect x="216" y="34" width="100" height="104" fill="#F3F8FF" stroke="#0047BA" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="93.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" fill="#0A1F3D">80</text><text x="328" y="93.0" font-size="20" fill="#0A1F3D">= <tspan font-weight="700">180</tspan></text><text x="36" y="181.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">3</text><rect x="46" y="138" width="170" height="74" fill="#F3F8FF" stroke="#0047BA" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="182.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" fill="#0A1F3D">30</text><rect x="216" y="138" width="100" height="74" fill="#F3F8FF" stroke="#0047BA" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="182.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" fill="#0A1F3D">24</text><text x="328" y="182.0" font-size="20" fill="#0A1F3D">= <tspan font-weight="700">54</tspan></text></svg>

steps.text: 180 + 54 = 234. Check: 234 is close to our estimate of 200. ✅

slides.tip: 18 × 13 = 234. Remember this one. It is our anchor example.

notes.do: Hands-on: on grid paper he draws an 18 by 13 rectangle, cuts a line after 10 across and 10 down, and colors the 4 pieces. He counts each piece by multiplying.
notes.say: Look: the top row is 18 × 10 and the bottom row is 18 × 3. Those two rows are exactly what the stacked method writes down.
notes.ask: Which row is 18 × 10? Which row is 18 × 3? How do we know 234 is reasonable?
notes.listen: Top row 180, bottom row 54. 234 is close to 200. If he adds only three boxes, have him count the pieces of paper: four.

slides.title: Partial products, stacked
slides.text: Now write the same two rows in a stack. Same math, less drawing.

steps.text: Step 1. Multiply 18 by the ones digit, 3: 18 × 3 = 54. Write it on the first row.
Step 2. The 1 in 13 is really 1 ten. Write a 0 in the ones place first. Then 18 × 1 = 18 goes in front of it: 180.
Step 3. Add the rows: 54 + 180 = 234. Same answer as the area model.

slides.tip: The 0 in the second row is not extra. It is there because you are multiplying by tens.

notes.do: He copies the stack onto paper, with the ones digits lined up in one column. Have him point to the 54 box and the 180 box on his grid paper.
notes.say: The first row is the bottom row of the area model. The second row is the top row. The 0 says: this row is tens.
notes.ask: What happens if you forget the 0?
notes.listen: You get 54 + 18 = 72, which is far from 200. The estimate catches it.

slides.title: Why the 0?
slides.text: Say it in your own words before we go on.
prompts: Why does the second row start with a 0?
Which box or row of the area model matches 54? Which matches 180?
How does the estimate help you check 234?

notes.do: He explains; you play the confused student. Say: 'I think it should be 54 + 18 = 72.' He has to convince you.
notes.listen: We are multiplying by 1 ten, not 1. 18 × 10 = 180. 72 is nowhere near 200.

slides.title: Your turn: 24 × 13
slides.text: Estimate first: 20 × 10 = 200. Stack it on paper, then type.

items.q: 24 × 13: what is the first partial product, 24 × 3?
What is the second partial product, 24 × 10?
items.no: The 1 in 13 is 1 ten. Write the 0 first.

items.why: 72 + 240 = 312. That is more than 200 because 13 is more than 10, but it is in the hundreds, so it is the right size.

notes.do: He talks through each step out loud as he writes. You only ask questions; you do not write for him.
notes.ask: Where did you regroup? Where does the 0 go?
notes.listen: In 24 × 3: 4 × 3 = 12, write 2, regroup 1, then 2 × 3 = 6, plus the regrouped 1 makes 7. Watch his pencil at the regroup.

slides.title: The standard algorithm: Malik's mural
slides.text: Now the real mural: 24 × 18. Estimate: 20 × 20 = 400. This one needs regrouping.

steps.text: Ones row. 8 × 4 = 32. Write 2, regroup the 3 (write a small 3 above the 2 in 24).
8 × 2 = 16. Add the regrouped 3: 16 + 3 = 19. The first row is 192.
Tens row. Cross out the small 3. Write the 0 first. 1 × 4 = 4, 1 × 2 = 2. The second row is 240.
Check. 432 is close to 400. ✅ Malik needs 432 tiles.

slides.tip: Multiply first, THEN add the regrouped number. Cross it out when you are done with it.

notes.do: Model it on the whiteboard, slowly, with the small regrouped 3 written in a different color. Then erase and have him do it on paper with you watching his pencil.
notes.say: Multiply, then add the little number. Never add first.
notes.ask: Why do we cross out the 3 before the tens row? Look back at your guess from the start of class. How close was it?
notes.listen: The 3 belongs only to the ones row. If it stays, he may add it again in the tens row (a very common mistake).

slides.title: Teach me: 26 × 15
slides.text: Estimate, stack it on paper, then type each step.

items.why: 30 × 20 = 600. The answer should be in the hundreds.

notes.do: He is the teacher now. He tells you each step and you write exactly what he says on the whiteboard, even if it is wrong. Let him catch it.
notes.ask: Is 390 reasonable if our estimate was 600?
notes.listen: Yes, it is the right size (hundreds). Rounding both factors up made the estimate high. 3,900 or 39 would not be reasonable.

slides.title: Bigger numbers, same steps: 136 × 12
slides.text: A 3-digit factor just means a longer row. Estimate: 140 × 10 = 1,400.

steps.text: Ones row. 136 × 2: 6 × 2 = 12 (write 2, regroup 1). 3 × 2 = 6, plus the regrouped 1 makes 7. 1 × 2 = 2. Row: 272.
Tens row. Write the 0. 136 × 1 = 136. Row: 1,360.
Add. 272 + 1,360 = 1,632. Close to 1,400. ✅ The area model shows the same two rows: 136 across the top, 12 down the side.

slides.tip: Line up the ones. Every digit stays in its own column.

notes.do: He copies it on paper. If his columns drift, have him turn lined paper sideways so the lines make columns.
notes.ask: How many partial products are there? Why only two when 136 has three digits?
notes.listen: Two rows because 12 has two digits (ones and tens). The length of each row comes from 136.

slides.title: Your turn: 213 × 14
slides.text: Estimate: 210 × 10 = 2,100. 14 is a lot more than 10, so expect a bigger answer, still in the thousands. Stack it on paper.

items.no: Multiply each digit of 213 by 4, starting with the ones.

items.why: 852 + 2,130 = 2,982. It is in the thousands and bigger than 2,100, just as the estimate said, so it is about the right size.
items.no: Second row: write the 0, then 213. Add the two rows.

notes.do: He does it on paper with no help. Watch the ones column line up.
notes.listen: Rows 852 and 2,130; total 2,982. If he types 1,065 he forgot the 0 (852 + 213).

slides.title: Be the checker
slides.text: Each problem has one mistake. Find it.

items.why: The 1 in 13 is 1 ten, so the second row is 180. 54 + 180 = 234.
no: 8 × 3 = 24 is right. The mistake is later.
54 + 18 is 72. The adding is fine; the row is wrong.
Estimate: 20 × 10 = 200. 72 is far too small.

choices: 34 × 6 should be 204. The regrouped 2 was never added.
items.why: 4 × 6 = 24: write 4, regroup 2. 3 × 6 = 18, plus the regrouped 2 makes 20. So 34 × 6 = 204, and 204 + 680 = 884.
no: 34 × 20 = 680. It needs the 0.
184 + 680 is 864. The adding is fine; the first row is wrong.
Check 34 × 6 again: 4 × 6 = 24. Where did the 2 go?
7 × 3 = 21 (write 1, regroup 2). 4 × 3 = 12, plus the regrouped 2 makes 14. 141 is right.
47 × 20 needs the 0: 940 is right.
Add the rows again, one column at a time.

notes.do: He checks each row himself on paper before choosing. He must say WHICH row is wrong and WHY.
notes.say: These are the three mistakes that cost the most points: the missing 0, the forgotten regroup, and adding the rows.
notes.ask: Which mistake would the estimate catch? Which ones would it NOT catch?
notes.listen: The estimate catches the missing 0 (72 vs 200). It does not catch 864 vs 884 or 1,181 vs 1,081; those are close. For those you have to recheck each step.

slides.title: Ordering tiles
slides.text: Estimate, stack it on paper, then type just the number.

items.q: Tiles come in boxes of 36. Malik orders 12 boxes. How many tiles is that?
items.why: 36 × 12 = 72 + 360 = 432 tiles. That is exactly enough for the 24 × 18 mural!

items.q: Each box of tiles costs $19. Malik adds a spare box, so he buys 13 boxes. How many dollars?
The art budget is $250. Can Malik buy 14 boxes at $19 each?
choices: No. 14 boxes cost $266, which is $16 too much.
no: Check 19 × 4: 9 × 4 = 36, write 6, regroup 3. 1 × 4 = 4, plus the regrouped 3 makes 7. So 76, not 56.
19 × 4 = 76, not 66. Recheck the regroup.
$266 is MORE than $250.

notes.do: He reads each problem aloud, says the estimate, then solves on paper.
notes.ask: What does the 36 × 12 answer tell Malik about his order?
notes.listen: 432 tiles is exactly the 24 × 18 = 432 the mural needs. Two different multiplications, same answer, and it makes sense.

slides.title: Words from memory
slides.text: No word list this time. Type the word.

items.q: In 6 × 9 = 54, the numbers 6 and 9 are called ________.
items.why: 6 and 9 are the factors. They are the numbers you multiply.
items.no: They are the numbers being multiplied.

items.q: In 6 × 9 = 54, the answer 54 is called the ________.
items.why: 54 is the product, the answer to a multiplication problem.
items.no: It is the answer when you multiply.

items.q: In 24 × 13, the rows 72 and 240 are each called a ________ ________.
items.why: Each row is a partial product, one piece before you add.
items.no: Two words. The second word is the answer to a multiplication problem.

items.q: When 8 × 4 = 32 in the ones column, you write the 2 and ________ the 3.
items.why: You regroup the 3 tens into the tens column.
items.no: It means carrying extra value to the next column.

notes.do: No peeking at the vocab slide. If he misses one, he says the word three times, then types it again.
notes.listen: Spelling counts. 'Partial product' is two words.

slides.title: Check for understanding
slides.text: On your own. Estimate, stack on paper, then type.

items.no: Ones row first, then write the 0 for the tens row.
Ones row: 115 × 3. Tens row: write the 0, then 115.

notes.do: Hands off. He works alone on paper and types. Note his first answers.
notes.listen: 448 and 1,495. Both right on the first try means he is ready for the Pathways Week 6 Math retake (see the teacher notes).

slides.title: Five steps, every time
slides.text: Big numbers are not hard. They just need the steps in order.

steps.text: 1. Estimate. Round to the nearest ten and multiply.
2. Ones row. Multiply by the ones digit. Regroup when you need to.
3. Tens row. Write the 0 first. Then multiply by the tens digit.
4. Add the rows. One column at a time.
5. Check. Is your answer close to your estimate? Then type it carefully.

slides.tip: Slow and right beats fast and wrong. Check your typed answer before you press Check.

notes.do: Open the course page together and read the task list for this week, one day at a time.
notes.say: Tonight: the after-class lesson and Show What You Know. A little each day after that. On Tuesday you retake Pathways Week 6 Math.
notes.ask: Say the five steps without looking.
notes.listen: Estimate, ones row, zero and tens row, add, check. If he skips the check, remind him: the check is where the points are saved.

slides.title: Malik's Mural: On Your Own
slides.text: In class you learned to multiply big numbers step by step. Now you do it on your own. Keep paper and a pencil next to you. Work every problem on paper first.

slides.title: Explain it out loud
slides.text: Say these to a grown-up, or say them out loud to yourself.
prompts: Why do you estimate before you multiply?
In 18 × 13, why does the second row start with a 0?
What is a partial product? Give an example.

slides.title: Review your words
slides.text: Say the meaning out loud first. Then flip the card to check yourself.

One piece of a multiplication problem. You find each piece, then add the pieces.
A smart guess you make by rounding first. It tells you about how big the answer should be.
To carry extra value into the next place-value column when a column makes 10 or more.

words.meaning: The stacked, step-by-step way to multiply bigger numbers on paper.

slides.title: Estimate, ones row, tens row, add, check
slides.tip: 234 is close to 200, so it is reasonable. Do these same steps on every problem.

slides.title: Estimate first
slides.text: Round each factor to the nearest ten.

items.no: 6 × 5 = 30. Now add the zeros from 60 and 50.

items.q: Estimate: 30 × 30 = 900. Which answer for 29 × 31 is reasonable?
no: 60 is 29 + 31. That is adding.
8,990 is about ten times too big. Look for an extra zero.
290 is only 29 × 10. It is missing a piece.

slides.title: Partial products: 43 × 15
slides.text: Estimate: 40 × 20 = 800. Stack it on paper first.

items.no: The 1 in 15 is 1 ten. Write the 0 first.

items.why: 215 + 430 = 645. It is less than 800 because we rounded 15 up to 20, but it is in the hundreds, so it is about the right size.

slides.title: Regroup carefully: 46 × 27
slides.text: Estimate: 50 × 30 = 1,500. Write the small regrouped numbers on your paper.

items.no: Multiply first, then add the regrouped number.

items.hint: Cross out the old regrouped 4 before you start this row.

items.no: Add the rows one column at a time.

slides.title: Three digits: 214 × 23
slides.text: Estimate: 210 × 20 = 4,200. Keep every digit in its column.

items.no: Multiply each digit of 214 by 3, ones first.

slides.title: Be the checker
slides.text: Check each row on paper. Then choose.

items.why: The 2 in 24 is 2 tens, so the second row is 700. 140 + 700 = 840.
no: 5 × 4 = 20 (write 0, regroup 2). 3 × 4 = 12, plus the regrouped 2 makes 14. 140 is right.
140 + 70 is 210. The adding is fine; a row is wrong.
Estimate: 40 × 20 = 800. 210 is far too small.

choices: 58 × 6 should be 348. The regrouped 4 was never added.
items.why: 8 × 6 = 48: write 8, regroup 4. 5 × 6 = 30, plus the regrouped 4 makes 34. So 58 × 6 = 348, and 348 + 580 = 928.
no: 58 × 10 = 580. It needs the 0.
308 + 580 is 888. The adding is fine; the first row is wrong.
Check 58 × 6 again: 8 × 6 = 48. Where did the 4 go?

slides.title: Malik's mural
slides.text: Estimate, solve on paper, then type just the number.

items.q: Malik's class paints 16 mural panels. Each panel uses 45 tiles. How many tiles?
The art club buys 23 jars of paint. Each jar costs $14. How many dollars?
A bigger mural uses 18 panels. Each panel has 125 tiles. How many tiles?
A paintbrush costs $2.50. A sponge costs $1.75. How much for both?
items.why: $2.50 + $1.75 = $4.25. Line up the decimal points: 50 cents + 75 cents = $1.25, and $1.25 + $3 = $4.25.
items.no: Line up the decimal points. Add the cents first.

items.q: Malik's sketch has 12 squares. The mural has 6 times as many squares. How many squares does the mural have?
Malik puts 50 tiles into rows of 8. How many full rows, and how many tiles are left over?
items.why: 8 × 6 = 48, and 50 − 48 = 2. So 6 full rows with 2 left over.
no: 8 × 7 = 56, which is more than 50 tiles.
8 × 6 = 48, not 50. Two tiles are left.
10 left over is enough for another row of 8.

slides.title: Use your words
slides.text: Type the word from memory.

items.q: A smart guess you make by rounding first is an ________.
items.why: An estimate tells you about how big the answer should be.
items.no: It is the first step before you multiply.

items.q: The answer to 18 × 13 is 234. The number 234 is the ________.
items.no: It is the answer to a multiplication problem.

items.q: The stacked, step-by-step way to multiply is called the standard ________.

sets.q: Round to the nearest ten. Estimate 41 × 29: 40 × 30 = ____
Estimate: 30 × 30 = 900. Which answer for 33 × 28 is reasonable?
no: 9,240 is about ten times too big. Look for an extra zero.
264 is only 33 × 8. The tens row is missing.
61 is 33 + 28. That is adding.

sets.q: Which two partial products build 36 × 24?
no: The second row needs a 0: 36 × 20 = 720.
36 × 4: 6 × 4 = 24, write 4, regroup 2. 3 × 4 = 12, plus the regrouped 2 makes 14. So 144.
1,440 is 36 × 40. The tens digit of 24 is 2.

sets.q: In 47 × 36, what is the second partial product, 47 × 30?

sets.no: Ones row, then the 0 and the tens row, then add.

sets.q: Someone wrote: 63 × 25 = 315 + 126 = 441. What went wrong?
sets.why: The 2 in 25 is 2 tens, so the second row is 1,260. 315 + 1,260 = 1,575.
no: 3 × 5 = 15 (write 5, regroup 1). 6 × 5 = 30, plus the regrouped 1 makes 31. 315 is right.
You always add the partial products.
Estimate: 60 × 30 = 1,800. 441 is far too small.

sets.q: Malik's next mural is 32 tiles across and 19 tiles down. How many tiles?
Each box holds 144 tiles. The school orders 15 boxes. How many tiles?
A number being multiplied is called a ________.
sets.why: A factor is a number you multiply.
sets.no: In 6 × 7, 6 and 7 are both one of these.

sets.q: Round to the nearest ten. Estimate 59 × 31: 60 × 30 = ____
Estimate: 30 × 40 = 1,200. Which answer for 27 × 42 is reasonable?
no: 69 is 27 + 42. That is adding.
108 is only 27 × 4. The 4 is really 40, and 27 × 2 is missing.
11,340 is about ten times too big. Look for an extra zero.

sets.q: Which two partial products build 45 × 23?
no: 45 × 3: 5 × 3 = 15, write 5, regroup 1. 4 × 3 = 12, plus the regrouped 1 makes 13. So 135.
The second row needs a 0: 45 × 20 = 900.
1,350 is 45 × 30. The ones digit of 23 is 3, so the first row is 45 × 3.

sets.q: In 56 × 43, what is the second partial product, 56 × 40?

sets.no: Ones row, then the 0 and the tens row, then add.

sets.q: Someone wrote: 74 × 18 = 562 + 740 = 1,302. What went wrong?
choices: 74 × 8 should be 592. The regrouped 3 was never added.
sets.why: 4 × 8 = 32: write 2, regroup 3. 7 × 8 = 56, plus the regrouped 3 makes 59. So 74 × 8 = 592, and 592 + 740 = 1,332.
no: 74 × 10 = 740. It needs the 0.
562 + 740 is 1,302. The adding is fine; the first row is wrong.
Check 74 × 8 again: 4 × 8 = 32. Where did the 3 go?

sets.q: The mural's sky has 28 rows with 17 tiles in each row. How many sky tiles?
A tile-setter lays 135 tiles every hour. How many tiles in 12 hours?
One piece of a multiplication problem, found before you add the pieces together, is a ________ ________.
sets.no: Two words. The second word is the answer to a multiplication problem.

sets.q: Round to the nearest ten. Estimate 72 × 19: 70 × 20 = ____
Estimate: 60 × 30 = 1,800. Which answer for 62 × 28 is reasonable?
no: 17,360 is about ten times too big. Look for an extra zero.
90 is 62 + 28. That is adding.
496 is only 62 × 8. The tens row, 62 × 20, is missing.

sets.q: Which two partial products build 64 × 35?
no: The second row needs a 0: 64 × 30 = 1,920.
64 × 5: 4 × 5 = 20, write 0, regroup 2. 6 × 5 = 30, plus the regrouped 2 makes 32. So 320.
3,200 is 64 × 50. The ones digit of 35 is 5, so the first row is 64 × 5.

sets.q: In 85 × 27, what is the second partial product, 85 × 20?

sets.no: Ones row, then the 0 and the tens row, then add.
Ones row: 306 × 4. Tens row: 0, then 306 × 2. Keep the 0 in 306 in its column.

sets.q: Someone wrote: 52 × 34 = 208 + 1,560 = 1,668. What went wrong?
no: Add the rows again, one column at a time.
52 × 30 needs the 0: 1,560 is right.

sets.q: Malik's class makes 24 small mural panels. Each panel has 36 tiles. How many tiles?
The school orders 18 boxes of tiles. Each box holds 225 tiles. How many tiles?
When a column makes 10 or more, you ________ the extra value into the next column.
sets.why: You regroup, or carry, the extra value.
sets.no: It means carrying to the next place-value column.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one. Only your first try counts. Estimate first, work it on paper, then type carefully.

questions.q: Round to the nearest ten. Estimate 52 × 38: 50 × 40 = ____
Estimate: 50 × 20 = 1,000. Which answer for 46 × 19 is reasonable?
no: 8,740 is about ten times too big. Look for an extra zero.
414 is only 46 × 9. The tens row is missing.
65 is 46 + 19. That is adding.

questions.q: Stack 37 × 24. What is the first partial product, 37 × 4?
Still 37 × 24. What is the second partial product, 37 × 20?

questions.no: Ones row, then the 0 and the tens row, then add.

questions.why: The 4 in 43 is 4 tens, so the second row is 1,160. 87 + 1,160 = 1,247.
no: 9 × 3 = 27 (write 7, regroup 2). 2 × 3 = 6, plus the regrouped 2 makes 8. 87 is right.
Adding the factors does not multiply them.
Estimate: 30 × 40 = 1,200. 203 is far too small.
The second row needs a 0: 125 × 10 = 1,250.
7,500 is 125 × 60. The ones digit of 16 is 6, so that row is 125 × 6 = 750.
125 × 6: 5 × 6 = 30, write 0, regroup 3. Keep adding the regrouped numbers. So 750.

questions.q: Another mural is 26 tiles across and 34 tiles down. How many tiles?
Tiles cost $12 per box. Malik buys 15 boxes and pays with $200. How much change does he get?
questions.no: Two steps: multiply to find the cost, then subtract from $200.

questions.q: The answer to a multiplication problem is called the ________.
questions.no: It is not the factor. It is the answer.

teacher.objective: Ethan multiplies 2-digit × 2-digit and 3-digit × 2-digit numbers accurately and on his own: estimate first (round to the nearest ten), set up the partial products from the area model (18 × 13 = 180 + 54 = 234), line up place value with the 0 in the tens row, regroup correctly, add the rows, and check the answer against the estimate. He also spots a wrong step in someone else's work and types the math words (factor, product, partial product, estimate, regroup) from memory.
materials: The class lesson on a laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
Grid paper (1 cm squares), scissors and 2 colored pencils
Lined paper turned sideways (the lines make columns) and a pencil
Whiteboard and two marker colors (one color just for regrouped numbers)
Packet (2 pages), printed: page 1 Friday, page 2 Sunday

plan.do: Class slides 1–2. He reads Malik's problem and guesses 24 × 18. Write his guess in the corner of the whiteboard.
Class slide 3. Facts and tens out loud, then typed (7 × 8, 40 × 6, 18 × 10, 30 × 20).
Class slide 4. He reads all 7 cards aloud, covers each one and says the meaning in his own words.
Class slides 5–6. Round to the nearest ten. He says every estimate aloud before answering.
Class slide 7. Grid paper: draw 18 by 13, cut after 10 both ways, color and count 4 pieces (100, 80, 30, 24). Group by rows: 180 and 54.
Class slides 8–9. He copies the stack, then explains why the second row starts with 0. You play the confused student who says 72.
Class slide 10. He talks through each step while he writes; you only ask questions. Answer 312.
Class slide 11. Model it on the whiteboard with the regrouped 3 in a second color, then he does it on paper. Compare 432 to his guess from 9:30.
Class slide 12. He tells you each step; you write exactly what he says, even if it is wrong, and let him catch it.
Class slides 13–14. 136 × 12 together, then 213 × 14 on his own (2,982).
Class slide 15. He checks each row on paper and names the wrong row and why: missing 0, lost regroup, adding the rows.
Class slide 16. 36 × 12 = 432 tiles, 13 × $19 = $247, and the $250 budget question.
Class slide 17. No peeking. A missed word is said three times, then typed again.
Class slide 18 on his own: 32 × 14 and 115 × 13. Note his first answers.
Class slide 19. He says the five steps. Open the course page and read this week's task list, one day at a time.

watch: Regrouping: watch his pencil right after the ones digit. The regrouped number must be written small above the next digit and added AFTER multiplying (8 × 2 = 16, then 16 + 3 = 19). If he adds first (2 + 3 = 5, then × 8) or drops it, say: multiply, then add the little number.
Old regroup marks: before the tens row he crosses out the regrouped numbers from the ones row, or he will add them twice.

The 0 in the second partial product: he writes the 0 in the ones place BEFORE multiplying by the tens digit. Writing 54 + 18 = 72 for 18 × 13 means the 0 is missing (the second row must be 180); ask, What is the 1 in 13 really worth?
Lining up columns: ones under ones, especially when one row has 4 digits (136 × 12, 214 × 23). Use lined paper turned sideways.

Adding the rows: he adds the partial products one column at a time and regroups in the addition too (141 + 940 = 1,081, not 1,181). The estimate does NOT catch these small adding slips, so he must recheck.
Typing the final answer: he copies the number from his paper exactly and checks it before pressing Check. Commas are fine either way. A wrong digit typed is a lost point even when the paper is right.
Rushing: if he answers in under 20 seconds on a 2-digit × 2-digit problem, or skips the estimate, stop him: say the estimate first, then go. Slow and right is the goal today.
Word problems: he missed 18 × 13 inside a word problem before but could do the bare problem. Have him write the number sentence (36 × 12) before he solves.

packet_key.answer: partial product (quotient is the extra word)
The second row is missing its 0: 27 × 10 = 270, not 27. 108 + 270 = 378.
Yes. 720 is in the hundreds, about the right size. The estimate 1,000 is high because 15 was rounded up to 20; 50 × 15 = 750 is closer. (An answer like 72 or 7,200 would not be reasonable.)

teacher.notes: For you only (do not share with Ethan): his Pathways Week 6 Math scores were 80, 63, 55, 66 and 76 (a fifth try scored 0 because of a technical bug; ignore it); they dropped as he retried, a sign of rushing or guessing on the multi-step procedure. He scored 100 on Multiplication Mountain, so his facts and the idea of the area model are solid, and this lesson connects that model to the stacked method. Most of his lost points were typed answers, so this lesson has many more typed answers than multiple choice. Finish: if he gets both exit-ticket problems right on the first try and handles the find-the-mistake round, finish by having him retake the Pathways Week 6 Math check (aim for 85). If you run out of time or he is not ready, it stays on his task list for Tuesday, after the after-class lesson and both Practice sets. Tonight he does the after-class lesson; it ends with Show What You Know (10 questions, 3 different sets for retakes, he needs 85). If he scores under 85, look at the Formspree missed list: a missing 0 or lost regroup means 10 minutes of stacked problems on paper at the start of next lesson, with him saying each step out loud; adding slips mean he adds the rows one column at a time and checks against the estimate. He can retake the check during the week and gets a new set each time. Reading: he never mastered Pathways Week 3 Reading (75, then 25 in September), so his task list has him retake it on Saturday (aim for 85). Check the Pathways Formspree log next week; if he is still under 85, go over arguments and evidence with him in the first few minutes of Lesson 2.

tasks: Wednesday (after class): do the after-class lesson. It ends with Show What You Know. Aim for 85.
Thursday: do the Practice set. Work every problem on paper first.
Friday: print the Packet and do page 1.

Saturday: retake Pathways Week 3 Reading (Making the Case). Read carefully and look back at the story for evidence before you answer. Aim for 85. If it is locked, type 1111. Then, on an index card, write these 5 words and what they mean from memory: factor, product, partial product, estimate, regroup. Check your card on the Word Power slide.
Monday: do the Practice set again. You get a new set of questions.
Tuesday: retake Pathways Week 6 Math. Estimate first and check every typed answer. Aim for 85. If it is locked, type 1111.
